strength: It finds all three signals and turns them into a clean budget that adds up to exactly ₹5,60,000: relaunch 'Dad's razor vs mine' with new cuts, cut the COD-trap Starter Kit, and split out women 25 to 34. A clear ASC ladder makes it runnable on Monday.
mistake: The main decision line is the ₹394 break-even on Meta's count, with the attribution-adjusted ₹282 kept only as a 'safe' line, and it scales Catalog DPA 20% even though DPA is only at break-even after the haircut and already at frequency 5.2.
to10: Set every target on the Shopify-adjusted break-even, project before-and-after profit for the new split, and add a prepaid nudge for the COD-heavy segments.

strength: Every verdict rests on store-count, after-RTO profit per ad set with the working shown, and it adds a before-and-after projection (−₹1,85,300 down to about −₹63,200) plus a sized prepaid lever (₹124 per switched order, ₹201 on the starter kit).
mistake: It closes the UGC test and moves its ad into ASC after only 5 days. It also asks for a sign-off on the prepaid offer and the pauses when the brief said I can't be reached.
to10: Commit to a specific prepaid offer, give the UGC concept a fair read before merging it, and keep the creative brief in our voice and our customers' words a bit more vividly.

strength: Every rule traces back to the money. It works out a $38 target from 90-day profit, sizes ad groups from learning-phase maths ($136 a day), and settles day 30 with three reads (tagged orders, survey, lift) where two must agree.
mistake: It picks calendar dates (23 Nov launch, Thanksgiving) and a ~$65k Meta monthly spend we never gave, and it only writes a full creator brief for new on-feet worker creators from week 2 onward.
to10: Add a short creator brief for 6 to 10 new on-feet workers (nurse, server, warehouse, retail) at launch, with hooks taken word for word from Maria's lines.

strength: A thorough, practical set-up (event-ID dedup, domain verification, comment moderation), a sensible way to handle price without discount hooks, and named Monday owners.
mistake: The day-30 scorecard doesn't say which source the cost per first order comes from, mixes a days 15 to 30 cost test with a 30-day order count, and opens scaling on day 8, before groups have learned.
to10: Make the day-30 verdict depend on Shopify, survey and lift reads agreeing at $38 or less, and hold scaling until groups have enough purchases.

strength: Very tight on claims: 'quiet', 'light' and looks appear only as quoted reviews. It pairs this with a concrete test plan (four ad sets, ₹1,100 a day, purchase-count cut rules, control ad) that I could launch tomorrow.
mistake: The primary text runs long and cites review counts ('290 of our reviews mention…'), so it reads like a report, not our short, calm, grade-7 voice.
to10: Rewrite the primary text in short brand-voice lines and add one genuinely unexpected concept, such as a price reframe, alongside the solid core.

strength: It spots that women get 18% of spend but bring 26% of purchases. Its copy is short and on-voice, and the per-trip maths concept (about ₹292 a trip) is a fresh idea I hadn't considered.
mistake: It puts 'Quiet wheels' and 'rolls quiet' in our own voice in concepts 5 and 8. That is a claim beyond the approved specs, which I explicitly said to avoid.
to10: Keep 'quiet' inside quoted reviews only, and give the test plan real budgets, dates and cut thresholds instead of 'at least 3x CPA'.

strength: The main hooks come straight from my customers' words: "It's 3 pm. You know what that means." and "My kids think this is regular soda." Taste always comes before the claims, and every ad ends on our line.
mistake: The hook test has no purchase threshold or budget sizing; "about a week" won't give a reliable cost-per-purchase call. The creator briefs also leave out deliverables, usage rights and safe zones.
to10: Keep these hooks, then add a purchase-count rule for calling winners and a deliverables-and-rights checklist so I can send it to creators as is.

strength: It is ready for production: each angle is tied to my cost-per-purchase data, it marks which lines must be exact, and it covers deliverables, safe zones, usage terms and a hook-test rule (20 purchases, about $520 per hook, cut above $32).
mistake: The 3 pm script opens on a generic "Wait. Not today." instead of the 3 pm line, and the game-day hook ("And yes, it's soda") is weaker than Marcus's own words. The TikTok disclosure is loosely worded as a "Paid partnership label", and the piece runs near or over the word limit.
to10: Open Ads 2 and 3 on the customers' own lines ("My 3 pm soda", "My kids think it's real soda") and tighten it to fit the word cap.

strength: Six truly different angles (transparency, taste, sugar, protein/texture, 4 pm, price) with a launch plan that changes only the primary text inside each pair, so every result is clean.
mistake: Pausing the ₹340 and ₹380 ads to fund the test is a reasonable call, but it doesn't check whether those ads still bring in profitable volume at our margin first.
to10: Tie the keep and cut lines to gross profit per order rather than just the best live CPA, and add one wittier headline for the taste angle in Aditya's 'brownie, not a supplement' words.

strength: A sharp read of the data (paused winner, untested taste proof, price objection) plus a thoughtful backup set in case legal blocks the review quotes.
mistake: Several texts repeat the '12 g protein, no added sugar' formula. Two angles are transparency and two are taste, with no standalone 4 pm angle. Each launch combo also changes the headline and description at the same time, which muddies what it tests.
to10: Make the six angles distinct, hold the headline and description steady across the tests, and give a concrete budget and duration so the test can reach purchase-level reads.

strength: The cash limit (about 10 flat notes) and the first-week break-in are both stated above the fold, and the 'What fits, in real life' scenarios use the '8 cards, still closes flat' proof in a calm, honest way.
mistake: It invents a capacity for the hidden pocket ('one more flat note'). It flags this, but it is still a capacity claim we haven't verified, the very thing we said not to overstate. It also gives Chicago buyers no inch measurements.
to10: Add inch conversions and keep the SEO title under 60 characters. Drop the made-up hidden-pocket figure and replace it with a short note on how we'll measure the effect on returns.

strength: The cash and break-in fixes are tied to the return numbers: 3.3 and 1.6 per 100 orders, a conversion guardrail and a fallback subtitle. It also gives inch measurements for US buyers and opens with Tom's own 'brick in my back pocket' line.
mistake: The break-in expectation isn't in the above-the-fold bullets, and the notes section pushes the total close to or past the 1,000-word cap.
to10: Put 'snug for the first week, then it settles' in a bullet or under the button, and trim the notes so the total stays within the word limit.

strength: Builds the series on the quiz split and the sunscreen click-to-order gap. Email 2 Version A pairs niacinamide with daily sunscreen for uneven tone, and Email 4 answers white cast and stickiness, using the dusky-skin review as proof.
mistake: Email 5 tells everyone to use the salicylic acid wash morning and night. That contradicts Version C, which tells dry and sensitive people not to start with an acid, and it overloads beginners.
to10: Branch Email 5 by skin concern instead of pushing all three products to everyone, and add a holdout test against today's single email so lift is proven.

strength: Ready to launch. It shows revenue per click (₹48 vs ₹20 vs ₹9), sets entry and checkout-flow filters, offers A/B subject lines with character counts, includes a submit-ready WhatsApp Marketing template, and plans a 50/50 test against today's email.
mistake: It invents a signer ('Mohit, Co-founder') for Email 5. Version A also doesn't tell dark-spot buyers to pair the serum with morning sunscreen, which is the core routine for that group. The sample-size claim of 4,700 per side to detect 18% to 20% is slightly optimistic.
to10: Add morning sunscreen to the dark-spot version, give a fuller answer on stickiness in humid weather, and replace the invented signer with a confirmed name.

strength: It ranks groups the way my data says to. The just-lapsed 68 to 90 days come first with no offer, then the 5,200 Monsoon Dark buyers. Every count is clean, the offers stop at 10%, and the subscriber restart is held until delivery is fixed.
mistake: The Monsoon Dark first email never names a replacement roast; it only asks how I brew. That breaks our 'name the farm or roast' rule, and the match is pushed back to step 2.
to10: Name the closest current dark roast in the Monsoon Dark opener, and show WhatsApp-reachable counts alongside the email reach.

strength: The drafts are ready to send with merge fields. The Monsoon Dark email names the blend and the roasters' pick, the subscriber track leads with date choice behind a delivery gate, and gross profit is worked out group by group, net of discounts.
mistake: It starts with the 91 to 180 day group and treats the 9,000 customers at 46 to 90 days only as a future day-28 nudge, so the cheapest people to win back get no win-back wave of their own.
to10: Make the 46 to 90 day at-risk group wave one with a no-discount reminder, ahead of the colder bands.

strength: It ranks every move in one unit (contribution points of revenue, divided by effort) and sets hard cut lines like '$94 cap after $940 spend', which turns the diagnosis into a plan my team can run on Monday.
mistake: Linen is pulled only from Meta, not from email campaigns, and the gain ranges for the email moves are working guesses stacked on guesses, so they look more precise than they are.
to10: Add the tracking check against store orders since the January move, pull linen from all promotion, and include one fresh idea for Sarah's 'touch it first' fear, such as swatches.

strength: Sharp diagnosis: we spend about 19% more for 11% fewer new customers. It also checks Meta tracking since the January move and offers a swatch sign-up that answers Sarah's real objection.
mistake: The moves are ranked with 'High/Medium' labels instead of real numbers, and the scorecard leaves contribution as 'set baseline, up every month' and flow share as 'pre-January level', so the key line has no target.
to10: Put every move into one gross-profit number with effort, set a hard contribution baseline and target, and add a week-by-week plan with owners.

strength: It builds bundle one on the top face wash + serum pair at a modest ₹869. Every profit figure includes RTO cost (₹130 × 40% COD × band rate) as well as the ₹70 shipping, and each bundle and the ₹599 line get clear break-even points.
mistake: It never treats COD differently: there is no COD fee, no higher COD bar and no prepaid-only free shipping, even though under-₹500 COD orders are refused 29% of the time. The lip balm is not used as a cart add-on to cross the threshold.
to10: Add a COD-specific rule (a COD fee or a higher free-shipping bar for COD) with the RTO saving worked out, and make the lip balm a cart add-on that lifts ₹400–599 carts over the line.

strength: The price ladder on the serum page (₹599 → ₹749 → ₹999) is smart, and the case against simply discounting the 1,033 pair orders a month the store already gets is thoughtful.
mistake: Its core profit maths leaves out RTO cost. The threshold sizing assumes only 6% of orders fall between ₹499 and ₹598, when an even spread of the 27% band from ₹500 to ₹699 gives about 13%, and that clashes with its own ₹699 figure. The add/pay/walk shares are made up, so the ₹3.4 lakh a year claim is shaky.
to10: Put RTO into every profit line, size the affected orders consistently from the band data, handle COD separately, and keep the lip balm as an add-on instead of a discounted main bundle.

strength: It puts the in-app checkout bug first with correct money (558 orders, about ₹34 lakh margin at ₹6,090 each), calls it a ceiling, and shows its sample-size working.
mistake: It runs every test on all devices with orders as the only main metric, so the mobile-only size picker and hero changes get diluted by desktop traffic, and it never uses add-to-cart as a faster primary read.
to10: Target the mobile-only changes at mobile traffic, use add-to-cart as the primary metric for top-of-page tests, and break down the funnel by segment to show where each leak sits.

strength: A correct stage-by-stage funnel table by segment shows in-app add-to-cart is normal and the leak is cart to checkout. Matching the roughly 4,130 in-app errors to the 4,800 lost carts nails the bug, sized at ₹34 lakh margin.
mistake: The review block appears both in the ship list (rating under the name) and in Test 5, which blurs what that test is measuring.
to10: Separate the reviews-up change cleanly from the hero test, and give each test's minimum detectable effect in rupees of gross margin, not just percent.

strength: It works out RTO cost by pincode group (₹2.7L, ₹3.0L, ₹5.5L, plus loss per COD order) and builds a tiered flow on it: tier 3 ships only after a yes, metros get no nudge, and prepaid discounts are sized to break-even refusal rates of 17% and 11%.
mistake: The after-hours fix is one away message with a single Track button, not a proper button menu covering size, exchange and COD, and there is no idea for adding evening agent cover.
to10: Add a buttoned after-hours menu (track, size, exchange, COD) and shift one agent into the 8 pm to midnight wave.

strength: Practical operations: a buttoned after-hours auto-reply, moving one agent to a 2 pm to midnight shift, quiet hours, and a sensible staged rollout of the hold from tier 3 to tier 2.
mistake: The prepaid nudge goes to every tier with no incentive, as a Utility template, so it ignores the pincode economics and risks a category rejection. RTO cost is slightly off (₹11.3L vs ₹11.2L) and never broken out in rupees by tier.
to10: Size and target the prepaid nudge by tier with the money worked out, add a missed-delivery template, and give the cart and size copy more Snitch boldness.

strength: It gives a clear verdict and rupee reason for every ad set, relaunches the paused 'Dad's razor vs mine' video first (worth about ₹65,000), and has a budget that sums to ₹5,60,000 with a 20% scaling ladder and numeric daily rules.
mistake: Several verdicts rest on Meta's own count (scaling Catalog DPA at frequency 5.2 even though it flags retargeting-type over-counting). It also offers no prepaid or COD fix for the Starter Kit, only a cut.
to10: Judge every ad set on Shopify-adjusted numbers alone, add a prepaid-only or COD-confirmation route to bring the Starter Kit back, and move extra money into women 25 to 34 instead of just holding their spend flat.

strength: It judges every ad set against Shopify-adjusted break-even (₹282 for ASC), shows the working, and adds a prepaid-versus-COD lever with numbers (₹124 per order, ₹201 on the Starter Kit) plus honest caveats on what the data can't prove.
mistake: It holds back ₹1,82,000 in a reserve gated at ₹282, a level ASC is unlikely to reach soon. The relaunched winner is therefore not scaled, and the answer ends with 'to confirm' asks and invented dates even though the owner is unavailable.
to10: Cut the length to the 1,300-word limit, commit the reserve with a realistic scaling gate, make the prepaid fix a concrete Starter Kit offer, and drop the approval requests.

strength: The set-up table (owners, dates, 'done when', no launch if the test order fails), the $38 target worked from 90-day profit ($38.46), and kill, scale and day-30 rules in dollars make it ready to hand over on Monday.
mistake: It is dense and probably runs past the 1,400-word cap, and its 'Feet first' group is the least tied to the data (Maria and Tasha's words); it also has no separate mission concept.
to10: Trim it under the word limit and add hooks taken word for word from Maria's and Tasha's phrases, while keeping the dated set-up and the two-of-three-reads day-30 verdict.

strength: Clean 90-day maths, a creative plan built on on-feet workers (including new warehouse and teacher creators) with price answered inside the ad, and a budget that sums to $30,000 with a reserve released only on performance.
mistake: The day-30 scorecard leans on cost per first order and a store-lift check against a flat Meta spend, with the survey only a secondary check, and the set-up list lacks dates, owners and 'done when' tests.
to10: Make the day-30 verdict rest on Shopify-based reads (tagged orders, survey, baseline or holdout) tied explicitly to the 90-day break-even, and give the set-up a dated checklist with pass tests.

strength: It is ready to hand over: every concept has awareness level, hook, format, visual, paste-ready text, headline, character counts and a single test. A costed 7-day test plan with kill and scale rules sits on top, and the sums check out (₹7,700 per ad set is about 5x the ₹1,515 blended cost per purchase).
mistake: It is well over the 1,500-word limit. Some padding, like the sizes block and the "never show a laptop pocket" rule, adds length without adding much.
to10: Cut it to the 1,500-word limit and add one more format that really differs, such as a creator-led or UGC concept, so the set is less dependent on shot-in-a-scene Reels and statics.

strength: It opens with a sharp reading of the numbers (women are 18% of spend but 26% of purchases, and the working for 63 extra purchases is correct). It also adds fresher angles: a creator selfie Reel for Meera and a per-trip price reframe for the ₹6,999 objection.
mistake: Some copy goes past the approved specs: "wheels that just glide", "looks good and rolls quiet" and "looks sharp" are stated as the brand's own claims. The ₹292 per trip line also rests on an unstated assumption about trips.
to10: Keep the fresh angles but quote quiet and looks only as reviews, and add a concrete test budget with kill and scale rules instead of a loose "three times blended cost per purchase" guide.

strength: It ties each angle to the data (taste test $26, swap $32, label $44) and adds a hook-testing rule with correct arithmetic (20 purchases x $26 = $520). Each script has a full shot list, hooks and a creator brief, and the price objection is answered in the 3 pm ad.
mistake: It clearly overruns the 1,300-word limit by adding creator contract terms, delivery specs and platform-safe-zone notes nobody asked for. It also forces 'exact' word-for-word claim lines despite the brief saying scripts are guides, and it only uses the 'A new kind of soda' line in one hook.
to10: Cut it to 1,300 words by dropping the contract and delivery sections, keep the claims in a guide-not-script style, and use the brand tagline in every ad close.

strength: It opens the 3 pm script on a 2:59 desk clock with 'It's 3 pm. You know what that means', and ends every ad on 'A new kind of soda.' That matches Dana's words and the brand voice, and it puts taste first with the label held back until after it.
mistake: The shared rules cover the approved claims and disclosure only briefly. The hook alternates change several things at once, and the per-hook test budget is vague.
to10: Trim the last few words to meet the 1,300 cap, give each creator brief its own claims and banned-words line, and add a numeric decision rule for the hook test.

strength: Six primary texts that are genuinely different angles (transparency, taste, no added sugar, protein and texture, 4 pm, price) in a blunt, witty voice. The launch plan is two clean pairs, each changing only the primary text, with a budget and keep/cut rules that check out (₹10,500 per ad buys about 36 purchases at ₹290).
mistake: It tells the owner to pause the ₹340 and ₹380 ads to fund the test, which is a bold call with no check on whether those ads feed other goals. It also holds back the live no-added-sugar and protein angles.
to10: Add a short fallback in case review quotes are not allowed, and soften the pause call into a staged shift of budget.

strength: Opens with a clear read of the past 90 days: the winner was fatigued, not beaten, and taste and texture reviews never ran. It also adds a backup plan in case review quotes are not allowed.
mistake: Five of the six primary texts repeat "12 g protein. No added sugar" as a tail, so the angles blur together, which is the sameness the owner hates.
to10: Let each primary text carry a single distinct hook, and drop the repeated protein and sugar tail from most of them.

strength: Every fact traces to the brief, with no invention. The cash limit appears as a number in the subtitle, a bullet, the table, the first FAQ and the line under the button. The page is backed by a returns calculation (44% of 7.5% is about 3.3 per 100 orders) and a plan to measure the result with a conversion guardrail.
mistake: The break-in note sits in the description, table and FAQ but not in the bullets or under the button. The explanation and measurement sections also push the total past the 1,000-word cap.
to10: Move the 'snug for the first week' note into a bullet or the line under the add-to-cart button, and trim the extra sections to stay under 1,000 words.

strength: The break-in note is in an above-the-fold bullet, the 'what fits in real life' scenarios are concrete, and the calm, honest 'we would rather tell you now' tone suits the brand. It also answers the gift question.
mistake: It invents that the hidden pocket takes one more flat note beyond the 10. That raises cash expectations and could add to the 44% of returns it is meant to cut. It also adds unsupported details such as 'parking meters' and the reason the slots are snug.
to10: Remove the invented hidden-pocket capacity and other made-up details, and add a break-in line under the add-to-cart button.

strength: It turns the click data into money per click (about ₹48 serum, ₹20 face wash, ₹9 sunscreen), splits email 2 by quiz answer, and gives the sunscreen fears their own email that quotes customers' words and the white-cast review.
mistake: The dark-spot version of email 2 sells the serum alone and never pairs it with daily sunscreen, which misses the core routine for uneven tone; the series is also likely over the 1,800-word cap, and it signs email 5 as an invented 'Mohit, Co-founder'.
to10: Add sunscreen as the second step in the dark-spot path, trim it to the word limit, and sign off as the team rather than a named person.

strength: It is tight and easy to use, with the quiz split, a dedicated sunscreen-questions email, discounted prices worked out correctly (₹359, ₹1,167), and a day-11 email that answers 'just tell me what to use' with a 3-step routine.
mistake: The day-11 routine uses the salicylic acid face wash morning and night and stacks three products, which contradicts the slow-start message; the 'Yes' on wearing the sunscreen under makeup is also unverified.
to10: Fix the routine so it starts with one product and uses the face wash once a day, add subject-line variants and a more specific WhatsApp template, and add one fresh angle beyond the standard sequence.

strength: It catches all three signals in the data: a separate Monsoon Dark track, a delivery-fix gate before winning back ex-subscribers, and the 46 to 90 day band treated as at-risk (it starts at 68 days with no discount). Each is backed by group sizes, email reach, a stepped offer and a worked ₹557 / ₹442 gross profit per order.
mistake: The 46 to 90 band is split by an assumed even spread, and the lift and break-even logic is rough (the 1-in-5 rule). The piece also likely runs over the 1,500-word limit and is dense in places.
to10: Trim to the word limit, state the break-even lift per group plainly, and add a Monsoon Dark draft that names the actual closest roast instead of leaving it as an open question.

strength: It gates ex-subscriber win-back on a delivery fix, has a Monsoon Dark track, and gives a clean worked table of won-back customers and gross profit that nets to about ₹8.5 lakh. It also adds a day-28 running-low nudge and offer tests such as free shipping versus 10% off.
mistake: It starts with the 91 to 180 day group and never targets the 9,000 customers at 46 to 90 days who are drifting now. It only adds a nudge for future orders, so the cheapest win is missed, and group C gets 10% off from the first message.
to10: Put the 46 to 90 day customers first with a light reminder and no discount, replace the {{placeholders}} with real copy, and base the lift and break-even sizes on the actual holdout counts.

strength: Every move is sized in points of contribution with low, likely and high cases and the working shown, ranked by gain over effort. A $94 payback cap drives the Meta cut, and a week-by-week plan and a scorecard with act-when thresholds sit on top.
mistake: It is dense and probably runs over the 1,600-word limit. The 13.6% and 7.8% contribution baseline rests on an assumed 54.5% first-order revenue split, and the plan targets down 11% on new orders, which is no improvement.
to10: Trim it to the word limit, flag the contribution baseline as an estimate more plainly, and add a fresher idea such as a swatch offer for Sarah's fear of buying sheets unfelt.

strength: It reads cleanly. The proven-versus-to-check table gives owners, methods and dates, the tracking check on Meta against store orders is included, and the swatch offer speaks directly to Sarah's fear of paying $200 for sheets she hasn't touched.
mistake: Ranking is mostly qualitative (High, Medium, Low), and some figures are loose or unexplained, such as the $23k to $41k per $100k cut. The contribution baseline is left as 'set in week 1', and there are no week-1 steps per move or act-when thresholds.
to10: Size each move in gross profit dollars or points with the working shown, set a numeric contribution baseline and target, and add trigger thresholds to the scorecard.

strength: The three bundles do different jobs (lip balm add-on, hair duo, 3-item routine). Each has profit and break-even worked out, and the reasoning about not just discounting the existing face wash + serum pair is sound.
mistake: The threshold maths rests on a guessed 6% of orders sitting between ₹499 and ₹598. The order spread implies about 13% (a figure also guessed, since it assumes even spread inside the ₹500 to 699 band), so the ₹28k a month gain is understated and uncertain. COD refusal is only lightly built into the threshold decision.
to10: Derive the affected-order share from the order-value bands, build RTO cost into profit per order, and consider a COD-specific or prepaid-only free shipping bar.

strength: The face wash + serum duo is bundle one, with Kavya's words. The money is rigorous: RTO is built into profit per order, the threshold is compared across ₹599, ₹699 and ₹799 with break-even walk-away rates, and the test plan has guardrails and stop rules.
mistake: The Two-Serum Pair is a stock-up deal, not a routine, and ₹1,079 is a stretch for budget-tight Ishita. The lip balm add-on, the second most common pair, is missed. The answer also likely runs past the 1,300-word limit.
to10: Swap the double-serum bundle for a lip balm add-on bundle, add a COD-specific threshold idea, and cut the length to fit the limit.

strength: It opens with the browser-split funnel table, leads the ship list with the in-app checkout fix sized correctly (about 1,860 checkouts, 560 orders, ₹34 lakh), and then sizes each test to the right traffic: mobile-only tests for mobile changes, and add-to-cart as the main metric for the hero image test, with checked detectable effects.
mistake: Test 3 and the EMI test leave placeholders such as [real rating] and [amount], and the first-image test bundles a hero swap with a reviews move, so the two effects cannot be separated.
to10: Fill the placeholders with draft trial and delivery copy, keep it clearly under 1,500 words, and split the hero image and reviews changes into separate reads.

strength: It shows its sample-size working (16pq/d², about 227,000 per arm), adds a 'why test, not ship' line for each test, and sets sensible stop rules, a server-side split and gross-profit-per-session as the ship call.
mistake: It runs every test on all devices with orders per session and a 10% detectable lift, including mobile-only changes like the size picker and hero image, which dilutes the effect. The hero test is also given four weeks and a 10% orders target with no data behind it.
to10: Scope each test to the device it changes, use add-to-cart as the main metric for the hero image test, and give each test its own split, run time and detectable effect instead of one shared line.

strength: It works out RTO cost by pincode group (₹27, ₹41 and ₹70 lost per COD order) and builds a different flow for each: tier 3 orders are held until confirmed, and the prepaid offer goes only to tier 2 and tier 3 and is sized by break-even (₹30 pays at 17% refusal).
mistake: Holding every tier 3 order until the buyer says yes risks losing real orders, and the cancelled template's 'order again any time' is a slight marketing leak inside a Utility template. The plan also runs somewhat over the 1,500-word limit.
to10: Add a staffing move for the 31% of chats that arrive after hours, and tighten the length to fit the limit.

strength: It handles chat volume well: the after-hours auto-reply has buttons, one agent moves to a 2 pm to midnight shift, and the bot takes the order-status load. It also adds quiet hours and a holdout for the prepaid nudge.
mistake: The prepaid nudge has no incentive and goes to everyone, not tier 3 harder, and there is no RTO money table by pincode group. The tier 3 hold is delayed by a 2-week pilot and a call step, and its 'pay now' template is labelled Utility.
to10: Give the prepaid nudge a margin-sized offer targeted at tier 2 and tier 3, and show the RTO rupees by pincode group.

strength: Every ad set is judged on the store's real order count (the 72% Shopify match) and after COD refusals. That shows the account lost about ₹1,85,000 in 14 days, not the ₹29,000 Meta implies. The ₹1,82,000 reserve goes to ASC only at ₹282 a purchase or better.
mistake: It shows next-period orders dropping to about 790 but never plainly tells the owner to expect fewer orders. It also only hints at fresh cuts of the 'Dad's razor vs mine' hook instead of ordering 2 or 3 new versions of it.
to10: Say up front that volume will dip at first and why that is the right trade, and order 2 or 3 new edits of the paused creator video alongside the relaunch.

strength: Very easy to read. It shows the Women Body Razor age-by-age losses, includes the 'never pause a winning ad to refresh' rule, and writes creative briefs in Rohan's and Ananya's own words.
mistake: It lets the team scale ASC at up to ₹320 a purchase and hold anything under ₹394, when its own store-count numbers say ₹282 is break-even. Raising Catalog DPA 20% at frequency 5.2, and running the losing UGC test another week at ₹25,000, also spend money that loses on real orders.
to10: Set every scale gate at or under the store-count break-even (₹282 for ASC), and do not scale DPA or extend the UGC test until they clear that line.

strength: The money math ($27.10 first order, about $38.50 over 90 days, $38 target) is correct and drives every rule, and the creative plan centres on on-feet workers, opens problem-first and closes with the mission.
mistake: The day-30 lift check compares new customers with the prior 30 days, with no seasonal adjustment. Mixing a Days 15 to 30 cost bar with a 30-day order count also blurs the verdict.
to10: Exclude current customers, cut the hooks more tightly from Maria's and Tasha's own words, and use a day-30 test that adjusts for seasonality with two reads that must agree.

strength: The measurement is rigorous: learning-phase budget math, a tracking-mismatch kill rule, current buyers excluded, and a day-30 verdict that needs two of three reads to agree (tagged orders, survey, seasonally adjusted lift). The hooks are written shot by shot in Maria's and Tasha's words.
mistake: It picks dates that launch the test into Thanksgiving and Black Friday week, when ad costs are inflated. It flags this, but a cleaner window would make the first read more trustworthy.
to10: Start outside the holiday spike, or set a holiday-adjusted target, and trim the copy so the team can scan it faster.

strength: Eight truly different concepts across sound-led Reels, a creator video, carousels, per-trip price maths and gifting, built on the right signals: quiet wheels, women's ₹1,058 cost per purchase, belt-skipping work flyers and light colours to avoid scuffs.
mistake: It drifts past the approved claims by stating 'Quiet wheels' and 'rolls quiet' as brand facts in concepts 5 and 8, and concept 3 puts data talk ('top theme in our 1,150 reviews') into customer copy, where it reads clunky and off-voice.
to10: Keep every non-spec benefit inside quoted review lines, and add a concrete test budget, a read date and cut/scale thresholds.

strength: It is close to launch-ready. Claims are disciplined ('quiet' and 'light' appear only as quoted reviews), headlines come with character counts, Reels safe zones are set, and the test plan is concrete: ₹7,700 per ad set, a day-8 read, and 6+/4–5/≤3 purchase rules. Women solo travellers are rightly ranked first.
mistake: Three of the eight concepts are statics, which edges back toward the static look I said is flat. It is also long and dense for a non-expert to scan.
to10: Turn one or two of the statics into a Reel or creator format, and trim the setup rules so the concepts stand out faster.

strength: It ties every angle to the cost-per-purchase and comment data, and it adds real production detail: exact-claim lines, platform safe zones, usage terms, and a hook-test rule with a $520-per-hook read and a $32 cut line.
mistake: Its main hooks mostly don't use the customers' own words. The 3 pm ad opens on "Wait. Not today." and the family ad on "Packing the game-day cooler." It also calls TikTok's disclosure a "Paid partnership label" instead of the branded content toggle.
to10: Open with the real comment lines ("This is my 3 pm soda now", "My kids think it's regular soda") as the main hooks, and end each ad on "A new kind of soda."

strength: Its hooks come straight from customer language ("My kids think this is regular soda", "My 3 pm soda"). Lines like "Still fizzy. Still sweet. Still my treat." sound like the brand, every ad lands on "A new kind of soda", and disclosure is named correctly for both Meta and TikTok.
mistake: The hook-test plan is thin: nine ads at equal budget for "about a week", with no purchase threshold or cut line. It also skips creator deliverables and usage terms.
to10: Add a test rule with a minimum purchases per hook and a cost-per-purchase cut line tied to the $26 and $32 benchmarks, plus a deliverables and usage-rights checklist for creators.

strength: It catches all three signals: the paused winner, the taste reviews and the ₹90-a-bar objection. It then builds a clean test where only the primary text changes within each pair, so every result is readable, and backs it with a budget plan that checks out (₹5,70,000 ÷ 90 = ₹6,333 a day).
mistake: The revived 'flip the pack' ad is paired with the protein headline instead of 'Ingredients on the front'. That is clean for the test, but it waters down the old winner's message in the one ad meant to show whether that angle still works.
to10: Add one more blunt, witty taste line in Aditya's words, such as a brownie-not-supplement hook, and explain why the transparency ad doesn't carry its own headline.

strength: It reads the data sharply: the winner was 'tired, not broken', the untried taste phrase is our best proof, and price is the stated objection. It also adds a sensible backup in case legal blocks the review quotes.
mistake: Almost every primary text repeats '12 g protein. No added sugar.', and two of the six angles plus two of the four launch ads are both transparency. The range I asked for shrinks, and the tests change headline and description at the same time, so I can't tell which part won.
to10: Give each primary text its own single proof, put a taste headline in the set, and hold the headline and description steady across compared ads so each test measures one thing.

strength: States the cash limit and the slot break-in up front, in a bullet, the table and the FAQ, and adds a candid 'What to know before you buy' section that sets honest expectations without sounding defensive.
mistake: The SEO title runs about 63 characters, over the 60 target, and the line under the button misses the chance to set the break-in expectation that drives early returns.
to10: Open with Tom's own 'brick in my back pocket' phrase, tighten the SEO title, and add a way to tell whether the copy actually cut cash returns.

strength: Builds the page on customers' words ('brick in your back pocket') and real review counts, gives inches for US buyers, and adds a measurement plan with starting return rates (3.3 and 1.6 per 100 orders), a conversion guardrail and a fallback subtitle.
mistake: The break-in note is left out of the bullets and the line under the button, which is where the people who return within a week would see it.
to10: Put 'snug for the first week, then it settles' into the slots bullet or the line under the button, and trim the explanatory sections so the copy stays well under 1,000 words.

strength: Each email does one clear job. Email 2 splits by quiz answer, Email 4 answers the white-cast and stickiness questions with the real review line, and the arithmetic (8.0/6.8/2.2%, ₹359, ₹1,167) is right.
mistake: Email 5 tells every non-buyer to use a salicylic acid wash twice a day plus niacinamide. That contradicts the 'don't start with an acid' advice to sensitive readers and the slow-start rule. Email 1 also uses 'brightening' and 'clear skin', even though only as contrast.
to10: Make Email 5 a reminder tailored to each person's concern instead of one acid-heavy routine for everyone, drop the off-brand contrast words, and add a holdout test to prove the series lifts the 18%.

strength: It turns the click data into revenue per click (₹48 serum vs ₹9 sunscreen) to justify the plan. Each step stays one product and slow-start, and the plain-text founder note on day 13 repeats each concern's single pick. Arjun gets a clean two-step routine.
mistake: The test claim is a bit optimistic: 4,700 per side gives only about 70% power to detect an 18% to 20% change. The dark-spot email also doesn't tie niacinamide to morning sunscreen.
to10: Add the sunscreen-every-morning line to the dark-spot version and give an honest test length (about 6,000 per side, or a longer run).

strength: It has a clean Monsoon Dark track and a delivery gate for ex-subscribers, and every value line checks out from ₹557 and ₹442 to one clear net figure of about ₹8.5 lakh.
mistake: It puts 91 to 180 days first and gives the 9,000 at-risk customers at 46 to 90 days only a day-28 nudge after future orders, so the cheapest group to win back gets no wave of its own.
to10: Make the 46 to 90 day group wave one with a no-discount reminder, and check whether each group's holdout is big enough to read lift on its own.

strength: It starts with the just-lapsed group and Monsoon Dark buyers with no discount. It splits ex-subscribers by cancel reason behind a 95% on-time gate, and it gives a break-even rule for the code (more than 21% of code orders must be true extras), a holdout size check, and the value of each point of repeat rate.
mistake: The Monsoon Dark draft sends people to a brew quiz without naming the closest roast still on sale, and the value is split across separate lapsed, subscriber and repeat-rate figures with no single total.
to10: Name the closest match to Monsoon Dark in the draft and add up one headline gross profit figure, net of discounts and WhatsApp cost.

strength: It spots the Meta–linen link and shows the payback math: $71 first-order contribution, about $94 eighteen-month value, Meta losing $27 per customer. The swatch sign-up offer goes straight at Sarah's fear of paying $200 for sheets she hasn't touched.
mistake: The ranking uses vague High/Medium/Low labels rather than one shared gross-profit number, so I can't see how much each move is worth compared with the others.
to10: Size each move in dollars or points of contribution and add a week-by-week list of what ships, with clear trigger points for when to act.

strength: It ranks every move in one unit, points of contribution with low, likely and high ranges and an effort score, and adds a 13-week ship plan with 'act when' triggers. I could run my Monday meeting off this tomorrow.
mistake: Some targets don't line up. Meta's week-13 target is $100 while the cap is $94, and the new-customer target of 'down 11% or better' is soft. The 13.6% baseline for a year ago is an estimate and the working isn't fully shown.
to10: Make the Meta target match the $94 cap, show the working for the 13.6% and 7.8% contribution baseline, and add one fresher customer-facing idea, like Output 1's swatch offer.

strength: Makes the face wash + serum pair bundle one at a modest ₹869. Every profit figure includes the ₹70 shipping and the expected RTO cost, and the working is shown so I can check it.
mistake: Lip balm, the natural ₹199 add-on, is not used as a bundle or cart add-on, and there is no COD-only threshold or prepaid nudge, even though RTO is in the maths.
to10: Swap the serum pair for a lip-balm cart add-on to cross the line, and add a COD-specific rule such as free shipping at ₹599 for prepaid only.

strength: A clear price ladder on the serum page and a well-argued case against a plain duo discount that would just give money away on 1,033 existing orders.
mistake: The ₹599 threshold maths rests on an unsupported guess that only 6% of orders sit between ₹499 and ₹598, when my 27% band suggests nearer 13%. Profit figures also leave out RTO cost, so the threshold verdict is shaky.
to10: Size the affected orders from the real band data, put COD refusal cost into every profit line, and use lip balm as a cart add-on instead of a main bundle.

strength: The funnel table by device and browser makes the in-app checkout bug obvious: 4,130 in-app pop-up errors against 4,800 lost in-app carts. It sizes the fix correctly at about 560 orders and ₹34 lakh gross margin a month and ships it first, with an A/A test.
mistake: It states the smallest detectable effect for each test without showing the working, so I can't check the 10% and 12% figures myself or learn how they were reached.
to10: Show the sample-size sum once, add stop rules and say how to treat COD orders, so I can trust and reuse the timings.

strength: It shows the sample-size maths (0.70% baseline, about 227,000 per version for a 10% lift in 4 weeks). It also adds practical safeguards an owner wouldn't know: server-side splitting, stop rules, counting only delivered or prepaid orders for COD, and waiting out the 100-night return window for the firmness test.
mistake: Test 5 judges a hero-image change on orders at a 10% detectable lift and lists add-to-cart only as a guardrail. Add-to-cart should be the main read for a top-of-page change.
to10: Use add-to-cart as the main metric for Test 5, with orders as the guardrail, and add the funnel-rate table by browser so the diagnosis can be seen at a glance.

strength: Solid, ready-to-submit set: a COD confirmation with a call and a 48-hour hold for riskier pincodes, shipped and out-for-delivery updates that tackle the 44% "where is my order" load, and a smart idea to move one agent to a 2 pm to midnight shift.
mistake: The prepaid nudge has no incentive and goes to everyone the same way, so it barely pushes tier 3, where half the RTO money is lost. Filing a 'skip cash, pay now' prompt as a Utility template also risks a rejection or a reclassification.
to10: Size a prepaid incentive by pincode group from the loss per order, and show me the RTO cost per group so I can see where the money goes.

strength: It works out RTO cost and loss per COD order for each pincode group (₹27, ₹41, ₹70) and uses that to set a ₹30 or ₹20 prepaid offer only where it pays, showing the break-even. It skips metros, ships tier 3 only after a yes, and skips proven repeat buyers.
mistake: The order-status reply says the order is "on its way" even before it ships. It also has no staffing or shift fix for the 31% of chats that come in after hours, only an away message.
to10: Add an evening agent shift or an after-hours response-time target to the scorecard, and make the order-status reply match the order's real stage.

strength: Decisive and owner-aligned: it relaunches the paused 'Dad's razor vs mine' video first, cuts Starter Kit and Gift Sets, narrows women's razors to 25 to 34, and gives a 14-day split that adds to exactly ₹5,60,000 with numeric daily rules.
mistake: The two-line break-even (₹394 and ₹282) blurs the verdict on some ad sets. Catalog DPA is scaled on the lenient line, and the claim of '₹65,000 lost' from the pause is more certain than the data supports.
to10: Judge every ad set on the Shopify-adjusted line only, add a prepaid or COD fix for the kit, and trim the length to the 1,300-word limit.

strength: Rigorous and honest: one worked break-even example, every row judged on the Shopify-adjusted count, a before/after table, and a useful prepaid-versus-COD lever worth ₹124 per order.
mistake: It holds back ₹1,82,000 as a gated reserve and ends with 'your yes before anything goes live', although the owner said they are unavailable and wants decisions. The relaunch of the best ad is not made the clear first move.
to10: Commit the full ₹5,60,000 with a clear Monday-first relaunch of the creator video, drop the confirmation request, and give persona-worded creative using Ananya's and Rohan's actual phrases.

strength: A complete, Monday-ready plan built on the right signals: on-feet workers as Spark Ads from day 1, problem-first hooks with the mission as a closing fact, no discount ads, a $38 target tied to 90-day payback, and a budget that sums to $30,000 with dollar-based kill and scale rules.
mistake: The day-30 verdict leans on TikTok-reported cost per order plus a new-customer lift check, with survey answers as only a back-up. It has no holdout or geo test, and its Hold and Fail bands are loosely reasoned.
to10: Make a holdout or survey-based read decisive for the day-30 verdict, write out the actual hook lines in Maria's and Tasha's words for each concept, and size the new-creator brief explicitly.

strength: Rigorous and specific throughout: a dated set-up table with owners, a test order that must pass before launch, ad-group budgets sized to the learning-phase math (25 purchases a week is about $136 a day), a nine-hook table in customers' words, and a day-30 verdict that needs two of three reads to agree (tagged orders, survey, lift) with a geo holdout as the fallback.
mistake: It fixes calendar dates around Thanksgiving and December and then plans as if that period behaves normally, apart from one line. It also runs close to the word limit and packs a lot into tables.
to10: Account for holiday-season CPM inflation more explicitly, give the new-creator brief a headcount, and trim some table text for easier scanning.

strength: Eight concepts that really differ in angle and format (sound-led Reel, carousels, a price reframe, gifting), with short, calm primary text in Mokobara's voice and the buyers' own words.
mistake: The per-trip price concept (₹292 a trip) is a weaker, more transactional idea, and the test setup is lighter and less specific than it could be.
to10: Add per-ad-set budgets and kill/scale thresholds, and one concept built for women that goes beyond a single lift moment.

strength: Production-ready detail (safe zones, headlines with character counts, a test plan with budgets and decision thresholds) tied to the ₹1,058 and ₹1,615 figures, and it keeps scuffed dark shells off camera.
mistake: Several concepts are static product-in-scene images with longer, feature-heavy copy, so it feels closer to the 'same ads, new headline' pattern, and it likely runs over the 1,500-word limit.
to10: Replace the static-heavy concepts with more varied formats, and make the copy shorter and calmer in brand voice.

strength: Three distinct angles (blind taste test, 3 pm swap with the price answered on camera, game-day family), each opening on taste rather than the label, with hooks that use real comment language.
mistake: Disclosure and the approved claims sit in a shared rules block rather than in each creator brief, and the hook-testing advice is thin (no purchase threshold or budget).
to10: Put the exact claims and disclosure steps in each creator brief, and give the hook test a sample size and a budget tied to the $26 and $32 cost-per-purchase figures.

strength: It ties each angle to the owner's numbers, marks the exact claim and price lines, and gives a concrete hook-testing rule (20 purchases per hook, about $520 at the best past $26 cost per purchase, with a $32 cut-off).
mistake: It runs well past the 1,300-word limit by adding contract terms, deliverable specs and a rationale table, and the main hook for the 3 pm ad ("Wait. Not today.") is less rooted in customer language than the alternates.
to10: Cut to the word limit by dropping the extras, and open the 3 pm ad on the customer's own line instead of a generic pour-and-stop.

strength: It spots that the paused 'Flip the pack' winner was fatigued rather than beaten, brings it back in fresh words, and adds a taste text built on the 26% review phrase.
mistake: None of the six headlines is about taste or texture, and each launch ad changes the primary text, headline and description together, so the tests are muddied (A vs C both test transparency).
to10: Add a taste headline and make each launch combination change one thing, so transparency versus taste is a clean test with the 4 pm angle given its own text.

strength: It covers exactly the six angles that matter (flip, taste, no added sugar, protein and texture, 4 pm, price). Its launch plan runs two clean pairs where only the primary text changes, and it sizes budget and decision rules from the real numbers (₹10,500 per ad buys about 36 purchases at ₹290).
mistake: It tells the owner to pause the ₹340 and ₹380 ads without weighing the risk. The 'dense and chewy, not chalky' headline is also written but never used in a launch ad.
to10: Use the texture headline in a launch combination and add a short note on how to handle the paused ads' audience overlap.

strength: Puts the cash number (about 10 flat notes) in the subtitle, a bullet, the table, the first FAQ and the line under the button. It also does the return maths (44% of 7.5% is about 3.3 per 100 orders) and sets a measurement plan with a conversion guardrail.
mistake: The line under the button omits the break-in note, so it does not help with the early 'too tight' returns. The FAQ also leans on review counts, such as '142 of our 400 reviewers', which reads more like data than Bellroy's calm voice.
to10: Put 'snug for the first week, then it settles' in the line under the button, and swap the review-count stats for plainer customer quotes in the description and FAQ.

strength: Warm, calm, honest Bellroy voice. The 'what fits in real life' scenarios (light day, full day, most it takes) and the honest 'we would rather tell you now than have you send it back' line suit the brand and the cash and trade-off problem.
mistake: It invents a fact: the hidden pocket takes 'one more flat note', and the FAQ presents it as true. It also says the slots are tight 'so cards stay put', which spins the break-in problem and is not in the data. The assumption is flagged, but the claim still sits in customer-facing copy.
to10: Drop the invented extra-note claim, keep the real-life scenarios, and put the break-in expectation in the line under the button.

strength: It reads the data well, with correct per-click revenue (₹48, ₹20, ₹9) and the sunscreen gap. It uses customers' own words in subject lines and hooks ("Which serum is for me?", "Just tell me what to use", "Every sunscreen makes me look grey") and gives A/B subjects and a ready-to-submit WhatsApp template.
mistake: It probably runs over the 1,800-word cap with its measurement plan and extra setup notes. It also invents a named co-founder signature, and the dark-spot email never pairs the serum with daily sunscreen.
to10: Trim to the word limit, drop the invented signatory, and make the dark-spot path a serum-plus-SPF routine with the strength named in the subject lines.

strength: It is calm, clean and within the word limit. The dark-spot email pairs the serum with sunscreen, and Email 5 gives a 3-step routine with correct bundle maths (₹1,297 to ₹1,167).
mistake: The Email 5 routine puts everyone on a salicylic face wash twice a day plus a serum, which clashes with its own "one product at a time" advice. The sunscreen email also claims it "gets more questions than anything else we sell", which isn't supported.
to10: Give a safer, concept-matched starter routine in Email 5, add subject-line variants that use the customers' phrases, and drop the unsupported claim.

strength: It reads all three signals in the data: a Monsoon Dark track, a delivery gate before ex-subscribers are contacted, and 46 to 90 days handled as at-risk. Behind that sit group sizes that reconcile, a 21% break-even for the code, and a 10% holdout with a sample-size check.
mistake: It is dense and likely runs slightly over the 1,500-word cap. The 'even spread' assumption for the 68 to 90 day group is also a guess.
to10: Trim it under the word limit and name the closest roast to Monsoon Dark, so the first message needs no later fill-in.

strength: It gates ex-subscribers on delivery being fixed, sets up a Monsoon Dark match track, and adds a day-28 reorder nudge and a hot-brew angle for cold brew buyers.
mistake: The value case rests on optimistic invented lifts (two orders per win-back in 12 months, 4 to 8% lift). Its claim that a 1.5-point lift is detectable on a 1,310 holdout is not supported, and there is no break-even test for the discount.
to10: Replace the merge-field drafts with finished copy, show the discount break-even, and use conservative, defensible lift numbers.

strength: A clear diagnosis that separates what is proven from what needs checking. It shows Meta is the cost problem, that each first order loses $33, and that Meta customers do not pay back over 18 months, and it adds a good swatch idea for Sarah.
mistake: The moves are ranked only as High, Medium or Low rather than by a gross-profit number, so the ranking is hard to defend. The week-1 steps are scattered across the plan instead of sitting with each move.
to10: Put a dollar or contribution-point estimate and a first-week step on each move, and add trigger rules to the scorecard so it says what to do when a line misses.

strength: Every move is sized in one unit, contribution points, with low, likely and high cases and the working shown. It estimates contribution after ads at 7.8%, adds an effort score and an overlap discount, and gives week-by-week owners and 'act when' triggers on the scorecard.
mistake: It is dense and probably over the word limit, and a couple of estimates are shaky, such as the 13.6% year-ago contribution and some email sizing. The Meta tracking check is also weaker than comparing platform purchases to store orders.
to10: Trim it to the word limit, tighten the assumed contribution figures, and add a direct platform-versus-store order reconciliation for Meta.

strength: It makes the face wash + serum pair bundle number one, with a modest ₹75 saving and Kavya's own words. It then works the money through RTO-adjusted profit per order, break-even upgrades and a break-even walk-away rate for the ₹599 line.
mistake: The third bundle is two vitamin C serums at ₹1,079. That is not a routine and does not match how people buy today, and it is a stretch for a budget shopper like Ishita. The lip balm add-on is also left out.
to10: Swap the double-serum bundle for a lip balm add-on or a body routine, and show a COD-specific shipping rule (for example a lower free-shipping bar for prepaid orders only).

strength: It uses the lip balm as a ladder step (serum, then serum + lip balm, then full routine). It shows a clear break-even for each bundle and explains why ₹699 is risky.
mistake: It guesses that only 6% of orders are affected by ₹599, but the data implies about 13%. The threshold gain (about ₹28k a month) rests on invented add-on and walk-away rates. It also never offers the plain face wash + serum duo, the bundle customers already built, and instead bundles a lip balm into a 'routine'.
to10: Make face wash + serum a straight modest-saving bundle, size the ₹599 band from the stated order spread, and bring COD refusal by order value into the threshold decision.

strength: It puts the in-app checkout fix first and sizes it correctly (about 1,860 more checkouts, about 558 orders, about ₹34 lakh). It also shows honest sample-size working: a baseline of 0.70%, about 227,000 sessions per arm, and a 10% detectable lift.
mistake: It uses orders per session as the main metric for every test and runs them all on all-device traffic. That dilutes the mobile-only size picker and the hero image, and the hero test is held to a 10% lift it is very unlikely to deliver.
to10: Match the metric and traffic to each test, for example mobile-only for the size picker and add-to-cart for the hero image. Show the in-app versus Chrome funnel split in a table, and spell out the brand-voice copy for each variant.

strength: A funnel table by device and browser makes the in-app bug obvious. It matches the 4,130 in-app errors to about 4,800 stuck carts, sizes the fix correctly (about 560 orders, ₹34 lakh), and adds an A/A test to get a clean baseline.
mistake: Test 5 bundles a new hero image with a reviews block, so a win cannot be attributed to either change. Some copy is left as blanks such as [real rating] and ₹[amount], and the sample-size working is stated rather than shown.
to10: Split the hero image and the reviews block into separate changes, show the sample-size calculation for each test, and fill the blanks with ready-to-paste brand-voice lines.

strength: A complete, usable flow set with sensible guardrails (quiet hours, 10% holdout, a staged tier 3 hold, an after-hours auto-reply and an agent shift moved to cover the evening wave).
mistake: The prepaid nudge goes to everyone after confirmation with no incentive and no pincode targeting, and the 'pay online' template is filed as Utility even though it is a sales push. The money is split by pincode group only in prose, so the high-risk tier 3 band gets just a cautious two-week pilot.
to10: Work the RTO cost per COD order by pincode group, then give tier 3 a firmer confirmation window and a sized prepaid incentive while keeping metro light, with the payment push kept out of Utility.

strength: It turns the RTO data into a per-group cost table (₹27 / ₹41 / ₹70 per COD order) and builds different flows from it: tier 3 ships only after a yes, prepaid offers go only to tier 2 and 3, and the ₹30 / ₹20 incentives come with break-even math.
mistake: The 48-hour auto-cancel for tier 3 could cost real orders, and the confirmation template says 'Usually arrives {{6}}', which edges toward a delivery promise. It does say to watch lost orders and loosen the hold.
to10: Add a human call step before cancelling tier 3 orders, and add the agent-shift change for the after-hours load.

strength: Every ad set is judged on store-count, after-RTO profit with the working shown (ASC ₹394 per order, ₹282 Meta-count break-even, −₹37,900). The money is gated to that line, and the budget adds up exactly.
mistake: Women 25 to 34 keeps ₹23,800 at ₹414 per purchase against its own ₹311 store-count break-even, with no explicit test-and-cut rule. The plan also commits only ₹3,78,000, so growth depends entirely on the reserve rule.
to10: Give the Women 25 to 34 relaunch and the 'Dad's razor' new cuts their own spend gates and expected cost, and add a sharper Monday checklist so the team knows the exact first actions.

strength: Clear per-ad-set narratives: an age-by-age loss breakdown for Women, a strong rule never to pause a winner to refresh, and good persona-based creative briefs in Rohan's and Ananya's words.
mistake: It scales ASC on a ₹320 gate and its reserve on ₹300, both above its own ₹282 safe line. It also scales Catalog DPA 20% at frequency 5.2, so it spends more where the store count says money is lost.
to10: Make the scale gates match the store-count safe lines, keep Catalog held rather than scaled, and treat the ₹65,000 'cost of pausing' as a hypothesis, not a fact.

strength: Tight unit economics ($27.10 first order, about $38.50 over 90 days, $38 target), a budget that adds to $30,000, and a creative plan built on the nurse and server Spark Ads with the mission line at the close.
mistake: It assumes the March licences cover the whole month without checking dates. Its day-30 incrementality test (store new customers up by 70% of TikTok's claim) is one rough read, with the survey as an afterthought rather than a scored read.
to10: Write each hook in Maria's and Tasha's own words and score day 30 on two or three independent reads that must agree.

strength: It is truly ready for Monday: dated set-up tasks with owners and pass/fail checks, and a learning-budget calculation behind four $200 groups. Day 30 is judged on three reads (tagged orders, survey against a 32% spend share, baseline lift) where two must agree.
mistake: Ad group 4 ('Feet first', cuff snap, lunch check) is close to the product-first style that cost $40 on Meta, and $800 a day of test spend rides on it from day 1.
to10: Replace the feet-first group with more on-feet worker creators (warehouse, retail, teacher) so all test money goes to the proven problem-first angle.

strength: It reads the data sharply and the numbers check out: women at 26% of purchases on 18% of spend, a blended ₹1,515, and the illustration of 63 more purchases at ₹1,300. It also covers all three signals: the quiet wheels, the women solo travellers and lighter colours to hide scuffs.

strength: It uses the actual signals well: dark spots lead the personalisation, beginners get slow-start guidance, and the weak sunscreen click-to-order rate gets its own objection-handling email.

to10: Make the WhatsApp copy product-neutral, add the 10% code consistently to each CTA path, and tighten the sunscreen email with one clearer texture proof if the product page supports it.

strength: It correctly spots the main data issues, especially sunscreen getting many clicks but few orders, and builds a clear objection-handling email around white cast and stickiness.
mistake: Email 5 pushes a generic 3-product routine with Salicylic Acid 2% to everyone, including dark-spot and sensitive-skin subscribers, which goes against the data and the beginner-first brief.
to10: Replace the generic final 3-step routine with personalised one-product or two-product paths, remove the off-brand 'brightening' wording, and keep every email to one calm, beginner-safe job.

strength: It reads the key signals in the data: Monsoon Dark buyers need their own track, subscription churn is a delivery problem, and recent lapsers should be approached before cold customers.

strength: It correctly sees that the win-back should fix the reason for lapse first, especially the discontinued Monsoon Dark and the subscription delivery issue.

to10: Rebuild the target order around the 46-to-90-day group, use exact opt-in reach rather than a 70% assumption, remove placeholders by naming the actual replacement roast, and make the lift and gross profit maths cleaner.

strength: It nails the real causes—Meta CAC, linen returns, and switched-off email capture/flows—and turns them into capped spend rules, owners, first-week actions, and a usable scorecard.

to10: Tighten the wording, trim the assumptions-heavy sizing, and add one or two customer-facing CRM/creative examples in Brooklinen’s voice.

strength: It gives a clear, owner-friendly diagnosis and correctly focuses on Meta, linen shrinkage, and the missing email flows without pushing discount-led growth.
mistake: The plan is less operationally tight: the ranked moves have softer impact sizing, fewer day-to-day rules, and less precise action thresholds than the brief asked for.
to10: Add quantified contribution impact by move, week-by-week owners and cut/scale rules, especially for paid media and CRM flow targets.

strength: It uses the strongest signal in the data, the face wash + vitamin C serum pair, and works the money after shipping and COD refusal cost instead of relying on AOV.
mistake: The third bundle misses the natural lip balm add-on opportunity and is less clearly a routine than the owner asked for.
