strength: It has a clean, customer-friendly ladder and correctly protects the vitamin C serum by recommending ₹599 rather than ₹699.
mistake: It skips the obvious face wash + serum duo as the lead bundle and its bundle profit maths mostly ignores COD/RTO, which the brief made central.
to10: Make face wash + serum the main routine bundle, treat lip balm as the cart add-on, and redo all margin and threshold maths after shipping and COD refusal cost.

strength: It correctly treats the Instagram/Facebook in-app checkout issue as a ship-now bug, sizes the upside at about ₹34 lakh gross margin per month, and ranks tests around the real customer blockers.
mistake: It applies one broad 4-week, all-traffic, 10% order-lift testing rule too evenly, instead of tailoring sample size and main metric more clearly for mobile-only or top-of-page tests.
to10: Give each test its own explicit traffic scope, duration and detectable effect, especially for mobile-only size and hero tests, while keeping the bug fix first.

strength: It reads the browser split correctly, calls the in-app checkout bug a no-test fix with the money attached, and gives each ranked test a clear metric, guardrail, split, runtime and MDE.
mistake: It leaves a few implementation blanks such as EMI amount and firmness rating, and Test 5 partly overlaps with the ship-now reviews change.
to10: Remove the remaining placeholders by wording them as dynamic values from the product/payment systems and separate the already-shipped review summary from the hero-image test.

strength: It catches the tier 3 RTO problem, adds shipping/out-for-delivery updates for the order-status chat load, and gives practical flows with timing.
mistake: The prepaid nudge is treated as Utility with no incentive, while the brief wanted a prepaid nudge/offer handled as Marketing, and the payment URL variable is wrong.
to10: Add a margin-sized prepaid incentive by pincode risk, classify it correctly, and tighten the templates so every variable and assumption is ready for submission.

strength: It puts money first, targets tier 3 COD risk hardest, sizes the prepaid incentive against RTO savings, and separates Utility from Marketing properly.
mistake: Some delivery wording says 'usually arrives' instead of 'expected date range,' and the final 'To confirm' section leaves a little homework despite the no-questions brief.
to10: Change delivery language to 'expected,' remove the final confirmation asks by turning them into stated assumptions, and add clearer after-hours buttons.

strength: Judges every ad set on Shopify-adjusted after-RTO profit in rupees, relaunches the paused 'Dad's razor vs mine' first, and splits out women 25-34 instead of killing the body razor.
mistake: Holds back 1.82 lakh in ASC reserve and commits only 3.78 lakh, which leaves a large share of the 14-day budget unspent and could undershoot the volume the owner wants.
to10: Commit closer to the full 5.60 lakh with a clear release ladder so the budget actually gets used while still protecting break-even.

strength: Two-line safe/break-even framework makes the attribution haircut usable, and the budget table adds up to the full 5.60 lakh with a clear ASC ladder.
mistake: Scaling Catalog DPA 20% contradicts its own frequency warning at 5.2, and the 'hold' on the UGC test risks carrying a 581 cost-per-purchase ad set past its natural cut point.
to10: Apply its own frequency ceiling to Catalog DPA and put a hard 7-day cut gate on the UGC test before committing more money.

strength: Built directly on the store's data: problem-first hooks, the two licensed on-feet worker Spark Ads from day one, and a day-30 bar of ~$38 per first order from the 90-day payback math.
mistake: The 90-day value shown as 'about $38.50' is off the owner's working ($48.40 minus about $9.90 = $38.50, but the owner guides to ~$38); minor, yet the day-30 scorecard uses $38 so the reader must reconcile two numbers.
to10: Tighten the creative hooks to Maria's and Tasha's exact phrases and spell out the March rights date explicitly in the kickoff list.

strength: Uses the data sharply: the ~25 purchases/ad-group math sets four $200 cells, session dates with a hard tracking gate, and three reads (tagged, survey, lift) before the day-30 verdict.
mistake: The budget table's phase totals don't add up ($5,600 + $5,600 + $4,000 + $4,600 + $10,200 = $30,000, which does add up, so no fault there); the real issue is that the schedule assumes a Thanksgiving-week holiday effect without store evidence.
to10: Tie the day-30 verdict to a single crisp number the owner can read at a glance and drop the speculative holiday-cost note.

strength: Built tightly on my data: the review quotes are the hooks, women 25 to 40 get a dedicated lift-it-alone concept, quiet wheels become a sound-led Reel, and the copy stays in our calm voice with only approved specs.
mistake: The test plan is slightly under-specified for a real read (7 days at ₹1,100/day may not clear learning phase per ad set, and concept 2's 'check your airline's limit' sits close to a guarantee-adjacent claim that needs legal sign-off).
to10: Tighter production-ready scripts (shot list and on-screen text per beat) and a test plan sized to real traffic so the first three picks can be judged with confidence.

strength: Sharp framing of the spend gap (women get 18% of spend but 26% of purchases) and a clean, well-argued first-three pick with a concrete money illustration.
mistake: The per-trip maths concept invents a ₹292 figure and a 24-trip assumption that are not in my data, and they are unapproved price-framing claims a customer could hold us to.
to10: Drop the invented per-trip maths, ground every hook in a real review line, and tighten copy to grade-7 short lines throughout.

strength: Every angle is justified straight from the owner's own numbers (taste test $26 at 33%, 3 pm habit 23%, price 15%) and the price objection is handled inside the script in the customer's own words.
mistake: Ad 3 puts a label-read moment at 22-32 s for Marcus, which edges toward the weakest opening the data warns against and risks feeling like the $44 label-read ad; the creative beats in Ad 3 also feel less naturally 'soda joy' than the other two.
to10: Sharpen Ad 3 so the label line is a throwaway mid-action beat rather than a framed 'read the label' shot, and trim the 'For every creator' section so the whole piece sits comfortably under 1,300 words.

strength: Tight, well-voiced scripts with an end-line brand tag ('A new kind of soda') and clean disclosure, easy for a creator to shoot and edit down.
mistake: It under-uses the data: no per-purchase numbers in the rationale and the hook-testing section is vague ('after about a week') where the owner wanted a cost-per-purchase rule with a benchmark.
to10: Add the money read (benchmark $26 taste test, $32 swap, $44 label) into each angle and the hook-testing playbook, and give the creator briefs the same exact-claim guardrails as the script body.

strength: Names the paused winner as fatigued not failed, brings it back in fresh words, and pairs it with the never-run taste proof from the reviews.
mistake: Quotes review lines as ad copy without a note that review quotes need permission, only addressed in a backup, and the 125-character assumption is stated more confidently than Meta's placement variation allows.
to10: Add a one-line legal/permission note on quoting reviews before launch and tighten the display-limit caveat to match Meta's placement reality.

strength: The test plan is unusually concrete: two matched pairs, budget sized to the past spend, and a numeric keep/cut line at ₹290 and ₹380.
mistake: The 2.5 frequency rule contradicts the data (old winner only tired at 4.2), and the ₹6,333/day math anchors budget to past spend without knowing margin.
to10: Justify the 2.5 frequency threshold against the observed 4.2 and tie the daily budget to gross profit per order rather than past spend.

strength: Cash capacity is stated as a hard number ('about 10 notes, laid flat') in the subtitle, a bullet, the table, the first FAQ and under the button, and the snug-slot break-in is handled honestly, directly attacking the 44% cash and 21% tight-slot returns.
mistake: It omits width and height entirely, so the front-pocket answer is thinner on proof than Tom's 'will it fit' doubt deserves, and the 'Not a fit if' line has no better-fit link.
to10: Add the missing dimensions and a sized front-pocket answer so the fit doubt is closed with numbers, not just thickness.

strength: The 'what fits, in real life' scenarios (light day, full day, most it takes) make capacity concrete for Tom and Jen in a way a spec table alone does not.
mistake: The subtitle and some bullets lean slightly long and marketing-flavoured ('wears in and looks better with use'), and its SEO title is well over the ~60-character target, showing less discipline on the stated limits.
to10: Tighten the copy to the brand's calm precision and bring the SEO title and subtitle inside the character and reading-level limits.

strength: It starts from the owner's real numbers — sunscreen clicks but doesn't convert, niacinamide does — and builds the flow and email 4 around the exact white-cast/stickiness objections, with each email doing one calm, on-brand job.
mistake: Sending the plain-text 'code ends tomorrow' note signed by 'Mohit, Co-founder' invents a specific person and signature the brief never confirmed, and the WhatsApp template uses placeholder IDs rather than Klaviyo-ready syntax.
to10: Confirm the code expiry, sign-off and WhatsApp opt-in as real, and give the WhatsApp template in submittable form with the actual variable mapping.

strength: Clear structure and a sensible branch by quiz answer, with a gentle short-routine email 5 that fits Arjun's 'just tell me what to use'.
mistake: Email 5 builds a fixed three-product routine and quotes ₹1,297/₹1,167 for everyone, which contradicts the 'one product, start slowly' advice and pushes all three products at beginners — against the brand's own rule and the brief.
to10: Keep the series one-product-at-a-time, fix the bundle pricing contradiction, and use the sharper sunscreen-click data as the organising insight rather than a flat summary.

strength: It catches both hidden signals — the stopped Monsoon Dark blend as the real cause for 5,200 lapsed buyers and the courier-driven late-delivery churn — and gives each its own track before touching discounts.
mistake: The messaging leans a little mechanical (group tables, gates) and the first-message drafts, while on-voice, don't quite land the warm, curious Blue Tokai tone in every line.
to10: Tighten the copy so every draft sounds like a person at Blue Tokai wrote it and add one genuinely fresh creative idea (e.g. a 'find your match' brew quiz series) rather than only offer logic.

strength: The copy is warm, specific and unmistakably Blue Tokai — naming the farm and roast, adding one brew tip, and the 'Now you pick the day your coffee arrives' draft is exactly the tone the brand wants.
mistake: The gross-profit case rests on assumed lift rates and a 2-orders-per-buyer assumption that isn't grounded in the data, so the ₹8.5 lakh figure reads as a forecast dressed up as a plan.
to10: Replace the assumed lift rates with a break-even/lift-scenario table tied to the ₹557 gross profit and show what each group must clear to pay for itself.

strength: Correctly isolates Meta as the cost driver, ties linen returns to wasted Meta spend, and ranks pausing linen plus the $94 payback cap as the top two gross-profit moves with owners, checks, stop items and a scorecard.
mistake: The $94 cap is derived from a rough 31% repeat rate math that the plan itself flags as an assumption, and some claim like 'up to about 1.8 points of revenue back' for linen conflates refunded revenue with gross profit gain.
to10: Tighten the linen impact estimate to show the actual gross-profit recovery rather than refunded revenue, and add a clearer first-week owner-by-day sequence so the team can start without interpretation.

strength: Ranks moves in a single contribution-point unit with low/likely/high ranges, shows the working for each sizing, and uses holdouts for email flows, which makes the plan measurable and board-ready.
mistake: It is dense and number-heavy, with many working figures and overlapping gain caveats that make it slower for a team to act on than it needs to be.
to10: Simplify the sizing tables to the two or three numbers that drive each decision, and give each move a plain first-week action that any owner can start Monday morning.

strength: Uses the real face wash + serum pair as the hero routine instead of discounting it, and pins the shipping move to ₹599 to protect the serum reorder.
mistake: The ₹599 threshold maths rests on an invented 6% slice and assumed 45% add / 40% pay / 15% walk split, and its ₹28k net is not tied to the brief's order bands, so the key saving is guessed rather than earned from the data.
to10: Redo the ₹599 calculation from the brief's actual ₹400-499 and ₹500-699 shares, show the margin and RTO effect per band, and let the lip balm cross-sell sit as an add-on rather than a serum bundle.

strength: Clean voice and a well-argued case for testing the shipping line, with a careful 15% walk-away break-even formula.
mistake: Bundle one is a two-serum pack that ignores the owner's top pair and the lip balm add-on, and the ₹599 table claims ₹1.08 lakh extra profit while also saying 2,370 orders lose free shipping — the arithmetic contradicts itself.
to10: Use the face wash + serum pair and the ₹199 lip balm as the real bundles, and rebuild the shipping table from the actual order-value bands with gross profit and RTO cost shown per band.

strength: Puts the in-app checkout bug first, sizes it honestly at about ₹34 lakh gross profit a month with the ceiling caveat, and ranks the five tests by evidence from the owner's own data.
mistake: The test maths is dense and a 10% detectable effect on all traffic still needs four weeks of two concurrent tests, so the calendar is ambitious and the owner may trip on the formula block.
to10: Give the ranked table the money each test stands to win in gross profit so the owner can see the order is ranked by rupee impact, not just by chat topic.

strength: Clearest read of the funnel by browser and device, with a sharp line on the pop-up errors nearly matching the in-app carts that never reach checkout, and a light 2-week test 5 on add-to-cart.
mistake: Test 5 bundles the hero image and moving reviews above the tiles into one test, so if it wins or loses the owner cannot tell which change did it, and the 6% detectable effect on a 4.0% add-to-cart baseline is optimistic for two weeks.
to10: Split the image and review changes into separate, cleanly measured tests or ship the reviews block without testing, and show the rupee impact of each ranked test.

strength: Builds the whole plan around the pincode RTO split, making tier 3 ship only after a yes and pricing the prepaid nudge off the real loss per order (₹30 in tier 3, ₹20 in tier 2), with the money shown.
mistake: Leans on a 'Confirm order' quick-reply gate for tier 3 that risks losing buyers who never tap, a risk it partly names but does not size against the delivered-order loss.
to10: Size the tier 3 confirm-gate against lost delivered orders and offer a callback path for no-reply buyers so the RTO saving is not eaten by silent cancels.

strength: Clean template set with quiet hours, an explicit marketing-opt-in caveat, a no-nudge holdout and a 2 pm-midnight agent shift that puts a person on the evening wave.
mistake: Skips the prepaid offer entirely ('sells ease, not a deal'), so the tier 3 buyer who is at 39% refusal gets no money-based reason to switch, and the ₹11 lakh saving is smaller than it needs to be.
to10: Add a tier-3-weighted prepaid incentive sized to the ₹180 RTO loss, submitted as Marketing, so the highest-risk band actually switches.

strength: Builds the plan on the real signals: the nurse and server Spark Ads from day 1, problem-first hooks, mission as the closer, no discount, and a day-30 check that also asks whether we own winning creative before the March licences end.
mistake: The day-30 new-customer test is a before-and-after against the prior 30 days with an unexplained 70% threshold, which is exactly the kind of pre/post read that flatters a Q4 launch, and it passes a days 15-30 cost bar while quoting a 30-day order count, so the pass line doesn't line up.
to10: Replace the prior-30-day comparison with a seasonally adjusted or holdout read, exclude existing customers from targeting, and make the day-30 cost and order-count rows use the same date window.

strength: Every rule traces to money and the store's own data: $27.10 first-order profit, $38.46 90-day payback, hook costs to the cent, the 13x and 7x median-view multiples, the 32% share-of-spend benchmark for the survey, and a two-of-three reads verdict that adjusts lift for last year's seasonal jump.
mistake: It commits to dated weeks around Thanksgiving without that date being in the brief, so the team could be testing a brand-new channel with unproven tracking in the most expensive week of the year, and the comment moderation and community staffing never gets an owner.
to10: Add the launch date to the 'to confirm' list with a fallback start, and give the social lead a daily comment and paid-partnership label check so the Spark Ads don't sit unattended.

strength: Every concept is tied to a real review theme or buyer group, with the quiet-wheels gap and the cheaper women 25 to 40 audience both given their own ad and put in the top three.
mistake: The test budget of about ₹7,700 per ad set buys roughly five purchases, nowhere near enough to separate ₹1,058 from ₹1,615, and there is no read split by gender, so the women-first bet cannot actually be proved.
to10: Size each cell to a read you can trust and specify a gender and age breakdown plus a store-order reconciliation before any scale or cut decision.

strength: The opening read is sharper than the brief: women 25 to 40 take 18% of spend but 26% of purchases, and the ₹292-a-trip reframe is a genuinely different angle on the ₹6,999 objection.
mistake: The rollout is not fundable as written: three cells under broad targeting with a ₹4,500 floor buys about three purchases each, so no concept can be judged, and it contradicts its own women-only concept while also spending on the ₹2,188 41-plus group.
to10: Give each concept its own audience and enough budget and a stated decision rule to produce a readable cost per purchase, and say what to stop instead of spreading to every group.

strength: Every spoken cell has a real line and the scripts themselves carry the signals — taste-test and swap openings, the '3 pm' line as on-screen text, and the $3 price answered in-scene — so a creator could shoot tomorrow.
mistake: The hook test is hand-wavy — 'run all nine at the same budget, after about a week' gives no spend per hook, no purchase threshold and no cut rule, so the owner cannot hand it to a media buyer as a decision.
to10: Turn the hook test into a money rule — spend per hook, purchases needed to read, and the cost-per-purchase cut line — so the scripts come with a decision, not just a plan.

strength: Opens with a why-this-angle table tied to the real view-rate and cost-per-purchase numbers, then backs it with a hook test that sets a $520-per-hook read and a $32 cut line, which is operator-grade.
mistake: Two spoken cells are left as directions ('their own words on why it works') and it ends with 'To confirm: creator fees and shoot dates,' asking the owner for information they said they could not give.
to10: Fill every spoken cell with an actual line and drop the closing 'To confirm' so the pack is complete on arrival.

strength: It reads the data the way I do — revives the paused ₹210 winner in fresh words, makes the untested taste proof (26% of reviews) the main challenger, and faces the ₹90-a-bar objection head on, with the historic ₹5.7 lakh ÷ 90 = ₹6,333/day spend turned into a real ₹1,500/day-per-ad-set test budget and 36-purchase sample.
mistake: It states Meta's display limit as "about 27 characters for each" for headlines and descriptions, which contradicts the brief's own guidance (about 40 and 30) — harmless here since every line still fits, but it is a wrong platform fact stated as fact.
to10: Fix the character-limit statement to the brief's 40/30 rule and put the taste headline into the launch set so the taste angle gets a headline as well as a primary text.

strength: It is careful and honest — review lines are quoted with their shares, the ₹90 a bar sum is shown, and it even provides legal-safe backup copy if review quotes can't be used.
mistake: The four-ad test is confounded: each ad changes primary text, headline and description at once, so the claim that "A vs C shows if the win came from the fact or from who the line speaks to" does not hold, and with no budget figures or explicit pause list I cannot run or fund it tomorrow.
to10: Hold headline and description constant inside each test pair so one variable changes at a time, give each ad set a daily rupee budget and a keep/cut line, and replace the second transparency text with a standalone 4 pm or protein angle so the six concepts are genuinely six.

strength: Cash capacity and break-in are stated as plain numbers in the above-the-fold bullets, and the 'What fits, in real life' scenarios (light day, full day, most it takes, what doesn't fit) make the trade-off concrete.
mistake: It puts an invented detail in customer copy (the hidden pocket holding one extra note) and leaves the front-pocket FAQ half-answered, so the page needs owner confirmation and a fix before it can ship.
to10: Answer the front-pocket question with the numbers in hand (10 mm at 6 cards, 14 mm at 12) and show the returns math and guardrail metric for the cash-return fix.

strength: It sizes the problem in money terms (44% of 7.5% returns = about 3.3 per 100 orders, tight slots about 1.6 per 100, 63% within 7 days), builds the copy against those numbers, and adds a conversion guardrail with a fallback subtitle.
mistake: It runs past the 1,000-word limit by adding measurement and rationale sections the brief did not ask for, and the repeated reviewer-count citations ('142 of our 400', '54 reviewers', '61 reviewers') make the copy read more like evidence-stacking than brand voice.
to10: Trim the appendix to a few lines and move the snug-slot expectation into an above-the-fold bullet so the 7-day returns are stopped before the scroll.

strength: It reads the numbers properly and builds the series around them: sunscreen's 2.2% click-to-order against niacinamide's 8.0%, three quiz-branched versions covering 55/26/19%, and one email that answers white cast and stickiness with the review line as proof.
mistake: Email 5 sends every subscriber, including the sensitive-skin group it told 'don't start with an acid', a twice-daily salicylic acid 2% face wash plus nightly niacinamide — two new actives at once, contradicting its own 'one product at a time, two weeks apart' rule in Emails 2 and 3.
to10: Make the day-11 routine segment-aware (one active per concern, matching each person's Email 2 version) so it never contradicts the slow-start advice, and spell out the WhatsApp message as a submittable Meta template with category, variables and sample values.

strength: It translates the funnel into money per click (₹48 serum, ₹20 face wash, ₹9 sunscreen) and keeps the whole series consistent — one product per concern in Email 2 and Email 5, one 10% offer only, and a WhatsApp template genuinely ready to submit.
mistake: Emails 1 to 4 open with no greeting at all, and the 'per click' figures are revenue rather than gross profit, so the only margin number in the document is the ₹70 code cost.
to10: Add the salutation to Emails 1-4 and put a gross-profit-per-recipient line next to each segment (net of the ₹70 code and RTO) so the owner can see what the series is actually worth.

strength: Separates proved from to-check with an owner, a deadline and a method on every open question, and it names the tracking gap (Meta's purchase count versus store orders since the January move) that decides whether Meta's $121 is real.
mistake: It ranks the moves on a soft High/Medium impact label instead of gross profit, and leaves the board's headline metric as 'set baseline in week 1 / up every month', so the scorecard has no contribution number to manage against.
to10: Put each move in one unit (points of contribution on revenue, with the working) and give the contribution scorecard a baseline and a week-13 target instead of 'up every month'.

strength: It converts everything into one currency - points of contribution on revenue - derives a 7.8% baseline and 11% week-13 target with the working shown, and gives each move a decision threshold, a holdout and an owner, so the plan can actually be run on a Monday.
mistake: The Meta sizing is about $2 light: at $110/$100/$90 per first order the share-weighted blended cost is roughly $101/$95/$90, not $99/$94/$89, and its tracking check never compares platform purchase counts to store orders, which is the gap that would prove or disprove the Meta number.
to10: Fix the blended-cost arithmetic and add the platform-versus-store order gap check, while keeping the one-unit ranking and the act-when triggers.

strength: It builds the whole plan on the browser split, and ties the 4,130 in-app pop-up errors to the 4,800 in-app carts that never reach checkout, so the bug fix and its money are argued from the data rather than asserted.
mistake: Test 5 bundles a new hero image with moving the review block, so a win cannot be attributed, and the copy still carries bracketed placeholders like the EMI amount and the firmness rating.
to10: Show the sample-size working next to each detectable effect (as a formula with the numbers plugged in) and split Test 5 into two clean single-change tests, or drop the review move to the ship list.

strength: The maths is shown and checkable (16 x p x (1-p) / d squared, the post-fix baseline of 0.81% needing 196,000 per version, and the 12-week desktop-only figure), and the operational rules on stop, split drift and sale weeks are what a team actually needs.
mistake: It gives every test the same 10% orders-per-session target, then admits an image change rarely moves orders that much, so Test 5 is designed to find nothing when add-to-cart would have read the answer in half the time.
to10: Tailor the main metric and detectable effect per test, using add-to-cart for the hero-image test with orders as the guardrail, so no test is sized to a lift the change cannot realistically produce.

strength: It turns my RTO table into money per pincode group, then sizes the prepaid nudge to the real saving (₹30 pays only if refusals there are 17%+), and it flags that cancelling unconfirmed tier 3 orders loses real orders, not just parcels.
mistake: It leaves three items in a 'To confirm' list (exchange window, reduced-amount payment link, per-message cost), so a few parts are homework rather than finished, and the COD template's 'usually arrives {{6}}' still leans on a courier date the owner may not want quoted at that step.
to10: Close out the open items with a stated default (7-day exchange, gateway capability, message cost) and put the metro/tier 2/tier 3 prepaid break-even numbers beside each offer so I can approve it without a follow-up.

strength: It is the cleaner read, and it catches two things I would have missed: that my checkout opt-in may not cover marketing messages, and that moving one agent to a 2 pm to midnight shift answers the 31% evening wave with a person instead of only a bot.
mistake: It drops the prepaid incentive and does not vary the prepaid nudge by pincode group, so the tier 3 towns that cause half my ₹11.2 lakh RTO cost get the same soft 'pay by UPI' pitch as metros, and that pitch is filed as Utility with a payment link whose URL variable is the customer's name.
to10: Tier the prepaid nudge with a margin-sized offer for tier 2 and tier 3 as Marketing, and fix the pay link variable and the tier 2 hold contradiction.

strength: Turns the brief into per-ad-set rupee verdicts, relaunches the paused 'Dad's razor vs mine' video first, splits out women 25-34, and lands a budget that adds to exactly ₹5,60,000.
mistake: Its two-line 'safe/break-even' framing muddles the very number that decides everything — the 72% UTM gap — so a few calls (Beard Kit 'hold', DPA 'scale') sit on shakier ground than presented.

strength: It quantifies each return driver in the owner's own units (3.3 and 1.6 per 100 orders), states a guardrail metric, and gives a fallback subtitle change if conversion drops — exactly the accountability a founder wants.

strength: Turns click-to-order into a money-per-click cut (₹48 serum / ₹20 wash / ₹9 sunscreen), uses that to justify the series structure, and answers sunscreen fears with the review line rather than pushing harder.

strength: It acts on every signal in my data — the discontinued Monsoon Dark blend gets its own match-led message, the courier problem gates the ex-subscriber track, and the 46-90 day drifters get a day-28 nudge — with gross profit worked from ₹557 and honest holdout maths.

strength: Splits proved from needs-checking cleanly and puts a hard $94 payback cap on paid with the working ($71 first-order contribution, $94 break-even with repeats) shown.

strength: Reads like a human wrote it, uses Sarah and Mike naturally, and adds fresh low-cost angles like a swatch offer and page fixes for returns reasons.

strength: It builds all three bundles from pairs customers already buy and does the full break-even and hazard-rate maths on the ₹599 threshold, protecting the hero serum alone.

strength: The ₹999 three-item Glow Routine refuses to simply discount the 1,033 pairs that already happen, and the state-by-state triage of ₹599 outcomes is genuinely useful.

strength: Puts the in-app checkout bug first as a no-test fix with the money sized (~560 orders, ~₹34 lakh gross margin), then ranks five evidence-tied tests with honest sample-size maths that admits page tests can only detect large lifts.

strength: Clean, well-evidenced plan that leads with the checkout fix and the ₹34 lakh gross-profit figure, and names the pre-fix baseline caveat (0.70% before, ~0.81% after the fix).
mistake: Applies a uniform 10% detectable lift to all five tests without adjusting to each metric's traffic and baseline, and ranks the hero-image test high despite admitting no chat data backs it.

strength: It correctly isolates Tier 3 as the RTO cost centre, builds a differentiated hold-then-ship flow for it, and backs every move with per-pincode-group money (about ₹5.5 lakh from Tier 3).

strength: Every element is tied to a pincode band and a rupee figure — it builds a tiered confirmation flow, offers the prepaid nudge only where refusal cost justifies it, and sizes the incentive (₹30/₹20) to the actual loss per order.
mistake: It leaves several items as 'To confirm' (exchange wording, reduced-amount payment link, message costs) rather than stating firm assumptions, so a couple of pieces are not fully paste-ready.

strength: Every rule hangs off the money: the $38 per-first-order target, the $57 stop line and a day-30 test that triangulates tagged Shopify orders, survey share and baseline-adjusted lift, so we don't take TikTok's word for it.

strength: Plain and easy to hand over: the set-up steps are practical (event-ID dedup, domain check, ads uploaded by Day -2 so review doesn't eat Day 1) and the 'we lose about $11 on the first order and earn it back on repeat buys' line makes the target obvious.

to10: Replace the platform cost-per-order pass mark with a Shopify-plus-survey read, fix the measurement window, and push more of the daily budget behind the nurse/server style.

strength: Every hook and script line is lifted from real review and survey language, and the first-three order is argued from actual spend and cost per purchase (women 26% of purchases on 18% of spend, 3x blended CPP as the kill bar).

strength: It is runnable as written: per-ad-set budget of 1,100 rupees a day for 7 days, day-8 decision rules, feed and Reels size with safe zones, headline character counts, and a platform-versus-store order check before scaling.

strength: Every angle and hook decision is tied back to the owner's own cost-per-purchase numbers, and the hook test gives a real money rule (about $520 per hook at $26 CPA, keep under $32), which a small team can run tomorrow.

strength: The cleanest, most natural-reading scripts of the two, with the 'A new kind of soda' tagline closing every ad and consistent rules that keep taste first and the label late.

strength: Brings the paused front-of-pack winner back in fresh words and pits it against the untapped taste hook in clean one-variable launch pairs, with decision math grounded in the actual past spend (₹5,70,000 ÷ 90 = ₹6,333/day, so ₹1,500/ad set funds it).

strength: Sharp strategic read plus a proactive legal fallback (backup lines if review quotes aren't cleared), and genuinely fresh angles like the 'label reader' voice and the added texture hook.

strength: Puts the cash number (about 10 notes) and the one-week break-in everywhere they matter, then shows the working — 44% of 7.5% = 3.3 per 100 orders — with a guardrail and a fallback line if conversion drops.

strength: It turns my data into money per click (₹48 serum, ₹20 face wash, ₹9 sunscreen), then restructures the series and the WhatsApp around that and around the quiz answer, with Klaviyo-level setup detail (entry filter, cart suppression, exit rule) I can hand to my team.

strength: It finds angles I would not have thought of - the swatch offer aimed straight at Sarah's fear of spending $200 on sheets she has not touched, and page fixes for each non-linen return reason - and it ties the Meta check to the January platform move.

strength: It puts the in-app checkout bug first, sizes it (about 1,860 extra checkouts, about 560 orders, about ₹34 lakh gross margin a month) and gives every test in exactly the format asked for, with on-brand lines like "Not sure? Try it for 100 nights."

strength: It turns the pincode data into money and action: ₹27/₹41/₹70 loss per COD order, tier 3 ships only after a yes, and the ₹30/₹20 prepaid offers are sized against the 17%/11% refusal breakeven.

to10: Size a real prepaid incentive for tier 3 (the owner's ₹5.5 lakh problem) with the refusal-rate breakeven, and fix the pay-link variable.

strength: It makes one rupee-reasoned decision per ad set and acts on the three real signals: relaunch the paused ₹250-ad first, split out women 25-34, and cut the Starter Kit COD trap.

mistake: It leaves the owner with homework — 'to confirm: your yes on the budget changes', the prepaid reward amount, and a ₹1,82,000 reserve that is only partly committed — so it reads more as a plan to approve than decisions already made.
to10: Commit the full ₹5,60,000 into named ad sets with a default prepaid reward amount, so the owner can hand it to the team on Monday without confirming anything.

strength: Builds everything on the two signals that matter — on-feet worker creators and problem-first hooks — and back-solves the day-30 bar from 90-day contribution ($38.46), with a concrete Monday set-up table and dollar kill/scale rules.

strength: Clean money first, correct hook cost table, sensible phase plan with a reserve, and a pass/hold/fail day-30 scorecard that includes a 'winning ads not on licensed posts' check — a smart guard against the March rights cliff.
mistake: It scales the bar to $45,000 on a pass without tying that to the 90-day payback math, and the $34 scale threshold contradicts the $38 target it just set, which an owner would trip over.
to10: Reconcile the $34 vs $38 scale threshold and justify the month-two $45,000 with the 90-day contribution math.

strength: Every concept is built on a real signal in the data — quiet wheels (290 mentions), women 25-40 at ₹1,058, lifting it alone — and the brief's numbers are used correctly to rank the first three.

to10: Lock the test budget to a learning-phase-safe number without asking the owner to confirm five things, and state the gross-profit math behind the ₹1,515 bar rather than only cost per purchase.

strength: Puts the money-first logic up front and ranks the first three well, with a clear per-trip maths concept that gives the owner a fresh price-reframe angle.

to10: Replace the invented per-trip maths with a claim that holds up, and give a concrete campaign structure with budget per cell and read dates instead of a loose 'three times blended CPA' rule.

strength: It reads the paused winner as fatigue not failure, brings it back in fresh words as the lead test, and pairs it against the never-run taste review phrase, which is exactly what the data is shouting.

to10: Give the taste review its own headline and description instead of burying it under the protein number, so the hook sells the idea, not just the primary text.

strength: It structures the launch as two clean message pairs with everything else held constant, so each test answers one question, and it budgets off the owner's real ₹5,70,000 spend with a rupee-per-purchase read.
mistake: It leaves placeholders for the owner to confirm (landing page price and stock, current review count) and the pairing logic ties each test to a fixed audience, so the price and taste tests are not cleanly separated from the segment.
to10: Remove the 'To confirm' homework and lock in the assumptions, so it is a complete paste-in brief rather than a plan that waits on the owner.

strength: It puts the 46-90 day drifters first, gives the 5,200 Monsoon Dark buyers their own track with a named closer roast, and gates ex-subscribers on a fixed on-time rate, all keyed to my data.
mistake: The three-month repeat assumption behind the subscriber and repeat-rate value lines is a bit loose and not separated from proven numbers.
to10: Show the break-even and value ladder from the holdout in one clean line so I can see exactly what lift pays for the programme.

strength: It asks for a day-28 running-low nudge and shows a full profit table with costs, which is genuinely useful for planning.
mistake: Drafts are full of {{braces}} placeholders, so I cannot send anything tomorrow without a developer, and the money numbers rest on assumed lift rates dressed as forecasts.
to10: Replace placeholders with real copy and put the 46-90 day drifters first, with a holdout-based break-even rather than assumed lift rates.

strength: It nails the core diagnosis (Meta drives the cost spike, linen breaks, paid email flows are switched off) and turns each into an owned move with a first-week step.

strength: Ranks moves in one unit (points of contribution) with low/likely/high sizing and a score, gives explicit act-when triggers, and holds out the flows for a real lift read.
mistake: Several working figures (7.8% contribution now, 13.6% a year ago, 54.5/45.5 revenue split) rest on an assumption that returning orders equal $188, and the 3-point plan is then planned off those estimates.
